scenes.title: Incremental Models in dbt
scenes.narration: This lesson explains incremental models, the dbt materialization that processes only new or changed rows instead of rebuilding a table from scratch.

scenes.title: Why incremental exists
bullets: Full table rebuilds get slow and expensive at scale
Most large tables only gain new rows each run
scenes.narration: Rebuilding a table materialization works fine until the table grows into billions of rows, at which point full rebuilds become slow and costly. Yet most large event or log tables only gain new rows between runs. Incremental models exploit this by processing just the delta, the new or changed rows, dramatically cutting both runtime and warehouse spend.

scenes.title: How an incremental run decides
steps: First run: build the full table
Filter source to only new rows and insert
scenes.narration: An incremental model behaves differently over time. On the very first run the target table does not exist, so dbt builds it in full. On every subsequent run dbt notices the table already exists, so instead of rebuilding it filters the source down to only the new rows and appends or merges them. This two-mode behavior is what makes incremental efficient.

scenes.title: An incremental model
scenes.narration: This model is configured as incremental with a unique key. The magic is the is_incremental block: it is skipped on the first full build but included on later runs. Inside it we filter the source to only rows newer than the latest timestamp already in the table, where the this keyword refers to the current model. The unique key lets dbt merge rather than blindly append, so reprocessed rows update in place instead of duplicating.

scenes.title: append versus merge

left.heading: No unique_key (append)
points: Risks duplicates if data is re-sent

right.heading: unique_key (merge)
points: Updates matched rows, inserts the rest

scenes.narration: The presence of a unique key changes the write strategy. Without one, dbt simply appends new rows, which is fastest but risks duplicates if the same data is ever sent twice. With a unique key, dbt performs a merge that updates matched rows and inserts the rest, making the run safe to re-execute at the cost of a little extra compute. For idempotent pipelines the merge behavior is almost always worth it.

scenes.text: Use --full-refresh after changing incremental logic, and set a unique_key so late-arriving or reprocessed data does not create duplicates.
scenes.narration: Two cautions matter here: run with the full-refresh flag whenever you change the incremental logic so the table is rebuilt cleanly, and set a unique key so that late-arriving or reprocessed data updates existing rows instead of quietly creating duplicates.
